||Agrivoltaic (AV) is a new concept integrating both the production of agricultural crops and electric power on thesame land area through the installation of photovoltaic panels some meters above the soil surface and the cropcanopy. In the present situation of energy demand from renewable sources, agrivoltaic systems with vines and/orfruit trees under the photovoltaic panels has still received poor attention. On the basis of this lack, the present 3-year study (2017–2019) aimed to investigate the effects of photovoltaic panels on grapevines of variety Corvina(_Vitis vinifera_L.). In particular, the experiment was carried out in a vineyard located in Northern Italy, Venetoregion, with the Corvina (_Vitis vinifera_L.) grape variety and the effects of shading by the panels on both phys-iological activities and vine performances were analyzed. Photovoltaic panels reduced both air and soilmaximum temperature by 1–2◦C. Vine transpiration on early morning was 0.83–0.90 in AV vs. 1.03–1.21 mmolH2O_m_−2_s_−1in full sun (FS) vines, whereas at midday values were signifcantly higher in AV vines (0.56–0.65)with respect to FS vines (0.38–0.44 mmol H2O_m_−2_s_−1). Photosynthesis followed the same pattern with valuessignifcantly higher in the FS vines at morning (9.34–11.03μmol CO2_m_−2_s_−1) with respect to AV vines(5.24–6–84 CO2_m_−2_s_−1), and the opposite was detected at midday, with 1.57–3.05μmol CO2_m_−2_s_−1in AVvines and 0.58–2.05μmol CO2_m_−2_s_−1in FS vines. The stem water potential was signifcantly reduced (lessnegative) by shading of the panels both at morning and at midday of values around 1–6 MPa thus indicating lessstressful conditions for AV vines. The photovoltaic panels affected the microclimate of the vineyard (lower airand soil temperature, higher soil matric potential) in the three seasons. Vine productivity parameters (yield,cluster number and weight) were infuenced to a limited extent; anthocyanins, TSS and polyphenols werereduced in grape must from AV vines. These fndings show that the panels affect the vines microclimate andphysiology and that yield reductions under AV are observed, but under hot and dry weather conditions resultscould be very interesting either for energy or fruit production. Further experiments need to be conducted in suchenvironmental conditions also in the perspectives of the climate change.|

## **1. Introduction**

Plant physiological activity is highly dependent on environmental factors such as air temperature and radiation that can affect leaf physiology and morphology in woody plants. Solar radiation availability depends on the time, latitude, local climatic conditions canopy characteristics, genetic and agronomic factors (Fanizza et al., 1999; Neri et al., 2003; de Villa et al., 2022). The physiological response of mature leaves to shade conditions is mediated by transpiration rate, as nutrients and hormone portioning to single leaves is dependent on the transpiration stream. Leaves exposed to high solar radiations usually transpire more

and receive a greater amount of resources than shaded leaves, although these latter can have an increasing role in buffering the adverse impact of climate change and extremes (He et al., 2018). The reduction of solar radiation can affect plant physiological activities by limiting photosynthetic activity (Cohen et al., 2005a; Wolz et al., 2017) due to reduction in stomatal conductance. Plant physiological activities are directly and ’s strongly influenced by the amount of solar radiation reaching the plant leaves with effects on stomata and temperature (Urban et al., 2017); any decrease of radiation might be expected to affect productivity (Cohen et al., 2005a; Wolz et al., 2017). However, some plants have considerable adaptability to different light regimes through changes in leaf

The capability of plants to adapt to different light conditions such as in greenhouses, under nets or plastic covers, has also suggested the possibility to use the photovoltaic panels above some agricultural crops. In a world where energy hunger is increasing, the use of renewable sources is necessary and the only sustainable way. The presence of the photovoltaic panels can ameliorate the microclimate of the vineyards in times of rising temperatures and water scarcity, even in areas where these problems were almost never faced, such as viticultural areas in the northern part of Italy. In this context, agrivoltaic (AV) systems can combine both food production and photovoltaic (PV) energy production on the same land (Dinesh and Pearce 2016; Weselek et al., 2019, 2021a). The technology offers a unique approach to produce energy by PV that can be used for smart irrigation system or for recharging electric vehicles for agricultural use. Furthermore, energy can be used for self-consumption in the farm for agricultural activities and in rural buildings in order to create the so-called energy communities with the neighborhood.

The photovoltaic panels can be placed some meters above the canopy in order to allow the cultivation of different crops and recent data report – that up to 60 70% of crop-available radiation can be maintained underneath the panels (Schindele et al., 2020; Trommsdorff et al., 2021; Weselek et al., 2021b). At the same time, renewable energy can be produced to support farmers’ income and face the increasing energetic demand of industries and cities (Dinesh and Pearce 2016; Schindele et al., 2020; Trommsdorff et al., 2021). The studies dealing with AV systems have generally focused on modeling (Amaducci et al., 2018; Elamri et al., 2018), and data obtained from field experiments are very limited and only regarding few crops (Marrou et al., 2013a; Weselek et al., 2019; Weselek et al., 2021a, b), with almost no information for fruit tree species or grapevine. Only in very recent years some applications for fruit trees such as pear (PV Magazine, 2020), apple (Juillion et al., 2022; Novuslight, 2021) or wine grape (Sun’Agri, 2021) have been started to be tested but data are very limited. But, apart from crops like lettuce (Marrou et al., 2013a; Cossu et al., 2020), corn (Sekiyama and Nagashima 2019), celeriac, winter wheat, potato, grass-clover (Weselek et al., 2021a, b) and other horticultural crops like pepper, strawberry, cucumber, rocket and tomatoes (Buttaro et al., 2016; Barron-Gafford et al., 2019; Cossu et al., 2020; Marrou et al., 2013b;), the impacts of AV can mainly be taken from modeling studies (Amaducci et al., 2018; Elamri et al., 2018) to be adapted to other horticultural species, including woody species which were poorly investigated. These limited studies showed contrasting results caused by the shade of the photovoltaic panels on the yield of the different crops, with reductions (− 5.3 to − 18.7%) in non-limiting conditions (Marrou et al., 2013b; Weselek et al., 2021a), but even to small increase of yield in hot and dry seasons (+2.7 to +11%) associated to a decrease in soil and air temperature (Weselek et al., 2021a). The photovoltaic panels did not reduce the yields of celeriac, a common root vegetable in Central Europe, after a two-year study (Weselek et al., 2021b). In general, a cover with photovoltaic panels ≤25% shade did not show significant effects on plant growth, whereas significant effects were noticed with coverage between 50 and 100% (Touil et al., 2021). Although a yield reduction can be detected in crops shaded by photovoltaic panels, we must balance the renewable energy generated by AV system, as in the case of yield reduction in winter wheat (− 18.7%) but with a production of 246 MWh, thus obtaining an overall production 56% higher than crop and PV production in two different sites (Weselek et al., 2021b). This should be considered when thinking AV systems to be established in marginal areas, abandoned lands and where hot and dry climates can occur frequently during the growing season, such as areas with Mediterranean climatic conditions. In this context, AV seems to be an appropriate approach to improve electrical self-sufficiency and independency from fossil fuels in the near future. However, considering the importance of fruit tree (including olive) and berry species for human consumption with an area of over 10 million hectares in the EU (27) for 2020

(FAOSTAT, 2022) and the significant amount of marginal and abandoned agricultural lands, the possibility of the application of AV systems is impressive. The importance of grapes for the production of table grapes, wine, and raisins is well known, and in the EU there are over 3 million ha devoted to grape cultivation, in different climatic conditions. Taking into account the noteworthy growing interest in AV systems towards a more sustainable world and the missing/limited data about the practical application of photovoltaic panels on woody crops (including grapevine), the aim of our study was to determine how wine-grape cultivation can be affected under photovoltaic panels with respect to full sun conditions. Results obtained from such researches could give hints for possible cultivation of this species (and others) under photovoltaic panels to produce energy for the community and agricultural products of good quality, in particular in areas where water scarcity is coupled with high insolation hours.

## **2. Materials and methods**

## _2.1. Experimental site_

Field trials were carried out during 2017, 2018 and 2019 growing seasons using vigorous, mature grapevines ( _Vitis vinifera_ L.) of cv. Corvina clone 48 that were planted in 2004 in open field under rain-fed system at the private farm in Valpolicella area (Northern Italy). Corvina grapevines were grafted onto SO4 rootstock and vine spacing was 1.0 m (within rows) × 3.0 m (between rows) trained to a pergola system under a typical Mediterranean climate with an overall height of 1.4 m (trunk height) and from 1.6 m to 1.8 m (canopy height). Vineyard was on flat surface located at Illasi (Verona province), 45[◦] 28[′] N and 11[◦] 11[′] E.

In the vineyard, 15 rows were covered by photovoltaic panels (AV plot) for 10 m long (10 vines/row) (Fig. 1) and all the measurements were taken from the central rows, 3 replicates each including 3 rows of 10 vines each whereas three rows used as borders. The panels were placed 2.6 m above the soil at the maximum high and 1.9 m at the minimum high, employing and raising the support structure of the vineyard, without much additional cost. The panels were installed in South direction. The shading determined by the panels was 75%, considering the distance of 30 cm between one panel line and the other. The panels were fixed and shielded the vines from the excessive brightness of the true midday sun.

A similar section of the vineyard, 5 rows distant for the AV plot was used as control in the full sun (FS). All the viticultural practices, including fertilization and pest control, were similar between the two plots and comparable to the standard agronomical practices adopted in the surrounding viticultural area. A typical Mediterranean climate with moderately cold and rainy winters and hot and dry summers is typical of the area. An iMetos meteorology station (Pessl Instruments GmbH, Werksweg, Austria) was placed near the experimental area, with sensors for measuring soil and air temperature, soil and atmospheric humidity, wind speed, solar radiation, and collected data were used to calculate ETo (using the Penman-Monteith equation). During July-August of 2019, climate sensors were also placed below the photovoltaic panels and in full sun: two MPS-6 soil water potential sensors at 30 cm deep; two VP3 environmental sensors located above the canopy to measure the vapor pressure, humidity, and temperature.

## _2.2. Vine measurements_

All the vine measurements were taken at two times of the day, morning (07.30–9.00 am) and midday (11.00–13.00 am) in the two plots, under the photovoltaic panels in the agrivoltaic vineyard (AV) and in the full sun (FS). The stem water potential (ψstem) was measured with a Model 1000 pressure chamber (PMS Instrument Company, Albany, OR, USA) in the morning and at midday in clear and sunny days on four different vines per replicate and on three mature leaves for each vine. Infrared thermography pictures were taken (at morning and midday) by using an infrared camera (Flir SC500/A40M, FLIR Systems Inc., Stockholm, Sweden) (Figure S1) with a built 24[◦] lens and the analysis of thermal images was performed using the ThermaCAM Reporter Software. The data obtained from pictures analyses were used to calculate the thermal indices for the vines. The index Ig is assumed to be proportional to stomatal conductance (gs) (Jones, 1999) and was calculated together with the Crop Water Stress Index (CWSI) as below reported:

Tleaf is the mean temperature of the transpiring reference leaf; Twet is the mean temperature of the water-treated leaf and Tdry is the mean temperature of the vaseline-treated leaf.

Gas exchange measurements were performed in the same days on fully developed leaves using a LCi-301 Portable Photosynthesis System (ADC BioScientific Ltd, Herts, UK). Instantaneous photosynthesis (A, μmol CO2 _m_[−][2 ] _s_[−][1] ), transpiration rate (E, mmol H2O _m_[−][2 ] _s_[−][1] ) and leaf temperatures were measured in the morning and around midday by double measurements on the same leaf from four vines (Medrano et al., 2003). The measurements were conducted at the following phenological stages: BBCH 75-Berries pea-sized, bunches hang; BBCH 77-Berries beginning to touch; BBCH 81-Beginning of ripening: berries begin to develop variety-specific color; BBCH 85- Softening of berries.

## _2.3. Yield, quality and composition of grapes_

Bud fertility was determined at flowering time by counting the clusters for each vine. The yield (kg/vine) and the cluster number were determined at harvest as average of the ten vines per replicate by using a portable scale. Harvest was accomplished on 20th September (2017), 30th September (2018) and 22nd September in 2019. The cluster weight was determined on the same vines as yield per vine/number of clusters. Three samples of 100 berry each per replicate were collected from

different clusters. Then, for each replicate, the 100 single berries were weighed and successively pressed, and the juice was analyzed for total soluble solids (TSS, expressed as%), pH, titratable acidity (TA, g/L as tartaric acid) together with tartaric and malic acids determination according to EEC 2676 standard procedure (OIV, 2019). Folin-Ciocalteu reagent was used to quantify the total polyphenols, according to the procedure described by Singleton & Rossi (1965) and briefly detailed in Ferrara et al. (2014). Total anthocyanins were determined using the bisulfite bleaching method.

After leaf fall, vines were pruned, and the pruned material was weighed in the vineyard with a portable scale. After pruning, the same number of buds (8) was left for each vine.

Analysis of anthocyanins was performed by HPLC using a Waters 600 E apparatus (Waters, Milford, MA, USA) that included a quaternary pump, a photodiode array detector (DAD) and an injection valve with a 20 μL loop. The samples, previously filtered on a 0.45 μm nylon membrane, were injected into a NovaPack C18 (150 × 3.9 mm, 4 μm particle size, Waters) column maintained at 30[◦] C and eluted at a 1 mL min− 1 flow rate with 10% formic acid (solvent A), and acetonitrile (solvent B). The gradient program of solvent A was as follows: 0–1 min 95%, 1–22 min 60%, 22–23 min 30%, 23–28 min 30%, 28–28.1 min 95%. Detection was performed at 520 nm, and quantitative analysis was performed according to an external standard method based on a calibration curve obtained by injection of solutions at different concentrations of malvidin-3-O-glucoside (R2 = 0.9993). Identification of anthocyanins was achieved by combining the elution patterns and data reported by other authors (Revilla and Ryan, 2000; Brar et al., 2008; De a Cruz et al., 2012). Results are expressed as mg of malvidin-3-glucoside equivalents per kg of grape.

## _2.4. Statistical analysis_

Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed with XLSTATProsoftware (Addinsoft, Paris, France) at the 0.05 P level. The assumptions of variance were verified with the Levene test (homogeneity of variance) and the Lillefors and Shapiro-Wilk tests (normal distribution). The mean values obtained for the different factors were statistically

separated by using the Duncan test at the 0.05 P level.

## **3. Results**

## _3.1. Microclimatic conditions in the vineyard_

The climatic conditions in the vineyard are reported in Table 1 for the three seasons. The weather data during the growing season reported drier conditions in 2017 during July and August (when we conducted the vineyard measurements) with respect to 2018 and 2019, with lower rain and higher evapotranspiration although VPD values resulted generally lower.

The climatic conditions that occurred in 2018 were characterized by significant rainfall during the growing season but the grapes reached an optimal maturation at harvest. The average temperature was around 25 ◦C in the period July-August (Table 1). Evapotranspiration values never reached such levels to induce water stress to vines and only in August 2017 ETo values were close to 4 mm per day. The average radiation during the three years was similar and in the range 160–175 W/m[2] .

In 2019, the average values of air temperature were similar in AV and FS, but the maximum values were always 1–2[◦] C higher in the FS plot during the hottest hours of the day in August (i.e., 14–18, 23–24) with respect to the AV values (Fig. 2). With regard of soil temperature, the values resulted always 1–3[◦] C higher in the FS with respect to AV during August (Fig. 2). Soil matric potential (Fig. 2) was higher (less negative) in the AV vineyard with respect to FS plot and the potential reduced more slowly under the shade of the panels, in particular at more negative values at the end of the growing season when air temperature was reducing.

## _3.2. Vine measurements_

The shade of the photovoltaic panels induced some significant physiological variations on the vines at two times of the day (Table 2).

Transpiration of FS leaves in the morning was significantly higher with respect to AV vines, varying between 1.03 and 1.21 mmol H2O _m_[−][2 ] _s_[−][1 ] for 2017 and 2018, respectively. Values of AV leaves resulted always lower than 1 mmol H2O _m_[−][2 ] _s_[−][1 ] in the three seasons at morning (0.83–0.90 mmol H2O _m_[−][2 ] _s_[−][1] ). Midday measurements showed a significant reduction of vines transpiration rate, with reduction in the range of 22–36% for the AV vines but up to 62–66% for the FS vines (Table 2). At midday E values were higher in the AV vines (0.56–0.65 mmol H2O _m_[−][2 ] _s_[−][1] ) and the transpiration of FS vines resulted 40, 27 and 28% lower than AV leaves for 2017, 2018 and 2019, respectively. The presence of the panels clearly modified the transpiration of the vines with an inversion between morning and midday for AV and FS vines. The E values resulted similar for the three seasons and for both treatments, with the exception of AV vines at midday in 2018 and FS vines at morning in 2017 (lowest values); moreover, transpiration was always higher in the morning with respect to midday values for either AV vines or FS ones (Table 2).

As observed for E, morning measurements showed that P values resulted higher in the FS vines varying between 9.34 to 11.03 μmol CO2 _m_[−][2 ] _s_[−][1 ] at morning in the three years; the AV vines did not exceed 6.84 μmol CO2 _m_[−][2 ] _s_[−][1 ] (2019) and resulted significantly lower in all the seasons (Table 2). However, at midday, the FS vines reduced the P by 94% in 2017 and 81–82% in 2018– than for the AV vines, 0.58–2.05 vs. 1.572019, with values significantly lower –3.05 μmol CO2 _m_[−] 2 _s_ − 1 (Table 2). The AV vines showed higher photosynthetic activity than those of FS around midday since the photosynthesis activity decreased to a lower extent with reduction of 70% in 2017 and 52 and 58% in 2018 and 2019, respectively (Table 2). The P values resulted similar for 2018 and 2019 and the lower values were recorded in 2017 for both treatments; moreover, P, as expected, was always higher in the morning with respect to midday values for either AV vines or FS ones (Table 2).

## _4.2. Effects of the photovoltaic panels on physiological parameters of vines_

Vine transpiration plays an important role in the energy balance of each leaf and is mostly affected by solar radiation and temperature. It is fundamental for canopy temperature regulation to prevent great temperature increase, especially in well-sun-exposed leaves, which need a higher latent heat flux to prevent an extreme temperature increase mainly in large-leaves species like grapevine (Lakso, 1994). The differences between the leaves of AV and FS vines at the two times of the day

were related to the high radiant load on the FS vines because of the higher temperature exposure during the hottest hours (12:00–17:00) of the summer days, whereas the AV vines had lower radiation exposure to the canopy during the same hours (Greer and Weedon, 2013).

In addition, the differences in leaf anatomy between sun-exposed leaves and shaded leaves may also play a role in the plant transpiration due to the variation of stomata density on the abaxial leaf surface which resulted 27% higher in sun-exposed leaves compared to shaded ones (Agati et al., 2008) or the specific leaf area (m[2] /kg), higher (≅ 23%) for leaves on shaded apple trees with respect to full sun trees (Juillion et al., 2022). With hot and dry climatic conditions, data at crop level below the photovoltaic panels suggest that these energy systems could contribute to save water, a very important resource in such environments (Marrou et al., 2013c). The water use efficiency in dry and hot environments was significantly higher for two crops, pepper and tomato, grown in an open field AV system (Barron-Gafford et al., 2019).

The reduced photosynthesis rate has been attributed to stomatal limitations (Shangguan et al., 1999) or thinner parenchyma (Gonçalves et al., 2008) and the photosynthesis reduction was recorded mainly in the leaves of FS vines at midday because prolonged exposure to high solar radiation (Gamon and Pearcy, 1990) and consequent reduction of vine metabolism at such radiations and temperatures. Greer and Weedon (2013) described the effect of high temperatures on reducing photosynthesis rate during the period of heat waves, both in protected and exposed vines, with greater and negative effects on exposed vines. This is highly consistent with the temperature-dependency of photosynthesis of vine leaves, which decreases markedly above 35[◦] C (Greer and Weedon, 2012a). Reduced photosynthetic activity (4.6 vs. 7.0 μmol _m_[−][2 ] _s_[−][1] ) has been reported for Semillon vines in lower light intensity conditions with respect to full intensity (Greer and Weedon, 2012b). The

Photon Flux Density (PFD) to saturate photosynthesis is temperature-dependent and a lower PFD is necessary to saturate in the cooler conditions of low intensity light environment (Greer and Weedon, 2012b). A recent work on the effects of shading nets and kaolin on Sauvignon blanc grapes reported significant lower values of net photosynthesis in shaded (30 and 70% shade) vines with respect to control ones in full sun (Cataldo et al., 2022). Research on Sangiovese have shown that leaf temperatures above 37–38[◦] C caused noteworthy reductions in photochemical efficiency, measured as the Fv/Fm ratio, (variable fluorescence/maximum fluorescence) and favoring the phenomena of chronic photoinhibition followed by chlorosis and necrosis of the tissues (Palliotti et al., 2007a, b). Salvucci and Crafts-Brandner (2004) also explained the reduction of photosynthesis because of the enzyme Rubisco activities limitation by high temperatures and radiation load. Some authors suggest that high temperatures either affect the enzymatic activity of Rubisco activase, an enzyme localized in the thylakoid stroma (Crafts-Brandner and Salvucci, 2000), or even the thylakoid membranes structure (Schrader et al., 2004). Osborn and Garrett (1983) ascribed the variations in photosynthesis, expressed on an incident radiation level basis, to differences in leaf absorbance. The leaves of the low-light-grown vines are generally well photosynthetically acclimated to these limiting conditions (‘shadow tolerance’), with reduced light saturation, maximum rates and a slightly reduced temperature optimum, as can be found in shade tolerant plant species (Greer and Weedon, 2012b).

The significant difference in ψstem observed between the two treatments was clearly caused by the shade of the photovoltaic panels which affected the water loss by reducing of light absorbance and favoring the stomatal closure (Chaves and Oliveira, 2004), since shade maintains higher level of leaf water potential comparing to sun exposed vines (Neri et al., 2003). In overhead shaded Shiraz vines, the midday ψstem was higher compared to control vines (Caravia et al., 2016), and higher values of water potential (ψleaf) were also found in shaded Sauvignon blanc vines (Cataldo et al., 2022) and in an agrivoltaic apple orchard (20% higher) in a three-year trial (Juillion et al., 2022) and the data of our trial are in agreement with these previous reports. The shade of the photovoltaic panels on the grapevines was able to keep the ψstem in a range of less stressful conditions both at morning and midday thus allowing the growth even in conditions of water reduction or limited irrigation, events both occurring in many viticultural areas of the world. Data obtained with the infrared camera suggest that the significant decline of stomatal conductance at midday compared to morning measurements can be explained by the increase of both air temperature and solar radiation, since stomatal conductance variations are related to canopy and leaves temperatures (Grant et al., 2007). High temperatures and intense radiations enhance stomatal closure to reduce light absorbance and minimize water loss (Chaves and Oliveira, 2004; Greer and Weedon, 2013) even before solar noon (Correia et al., 1990).

The CWSI values can be used as indicators to monitor the crop water stress conditions based on the leaf temperature (Ru et al., 2020) and data can be obtained either with proximal or remote distance measurements. Our data confirmed the effects of the photovoltaic panels in attenuating the negative effects of high temperatures on the vines water status since seasonal mean CWSI values resulted significantly lower for fully irrigated vines with respect to vines managed with reduced irrigation (60%) in different phenological stages, 0.18 vs. 0.68 (Ru et al., 2020). The applicability of CWSI has been often tested with ψstem (Gonzalez-Dugo et al., 2013) and relationships between these indexes in grapevine resulted either linear or curvilinear (Bellvert et al., 2015).

The architecture of the vine canopy can influence leaf temperature either because of the position of the leaves towards the sun light or the self-shading of each leaf in the canopy (Pearcy et al., 2004) and variation in the degree of shading could greatly affect the leaf temperature of each leaf (Boissard et al., 1990) and consequently stomatal conductance. Thermal imaging can provide a useful measure of the crop water status and is correlated with methods for estimating crop water stress.

Temperature-based indices calculated from data extracted from thermal images led to similar results to those obtained from direct measurements on grapevine leaves, separating shaded and full sun vines in the same water condition (Cohen et al., 2005b).

## _4.3. Effects of photovoltaic panels on yield, quality and composition of grapes_

The decrease of the yield in AV vines can be explained by the unfavorable microclimatic conditions in the shaded canopy due to reduction of the light interception and subsequent carbon assimilation, which may vary diurnally, daily and seasonally (Wagenmakeres, 1991; Dokoozlian and Kliewer 1995). However, a 30% and 50% of shade with sun tracking PV panels (4 m above ground) did not show any significant effect on lettuce production (Valle et al. 2017). Same results were also obtained under fixed panels with same covering ratio for the same vegetable crop (Marrou et al., 2013a). Photovoltaic panels, at two different densities, – even increased the production of durum wheat by 35 72% with respect to full sun in a trial in France (Dupraz et al., 2011). A recent study in Japan on corn growth cultivated under photovoltaic panels placed at two different densities (0.71 and 1.67 m apart) reported even higher yield with respect to control, taking also into account that corn is a typical shade-intolerant crop (Sekiyama and Nagashima, 2019). In an agrivoltaic apple orchard the sun tracking panels lowered flower intensity by 31% and the alternate bearing was also much reduced (Juillion et al., 2022). Although these data are mainly on vegetable crops, permanent crops such as grape or other fruit tree species (i.e., apples) can be cultivated under panels with steady yields although generally lower than in uncovered open field (Juillion et al., 2022). The annual revenue (energy plus harvested corn) resulted 8.3 and 4.7 times higher than control, respectively, for the high and low-density panel system (Sekiyama and Nagashima, 2019). Lettuce cultivated under 25 and 50% photovoltaic coverage showed a yield of 99 and 79%, respectively, with respect to the control (Marrou et al., 2013b). In our trial we observed a decrease in grape yield, at least in two years, but different results are reported by other authors (Dupraz et al., 2011; Sekiyama and Nagashima, 2019). Reduction (11–20%) of the yield of Semillon grapes have been reported for vines at low light intensity (30%) grown in Australia (Greer and Weedon, 2012b). This condition may be explained by various factors such as the light saturation point of the crop, and in areas with a high level of radiation a lower solar irradiance is sufficient to achieve the optimal photosynthetic rate; moreover, the photovoltaic panels can reduce evapotranspiration with their shade (Sekiyama and Nagashima, 2019) as observed in our study. The effects of the shade caused by the photovoltaic panels can be different with some negative effects on shade intolerant species and no effects or even positive on shade tolerant species (Trommsdorff et al., 2021). In hot climatic conditions the yield of the shaded strawberries was 1.2 times higher than that of the unshaded plants (Tang et al., 2020). To our knowledge, this is the first report on grapevine yield under photovoltaic panels after a three-year study and results are definitely promising to be applied even to other species but taking into account both positive and negative effects.

In a Shiraz vineyard in Australia, a heavier berry mass was found for the overhead shaded vines (62% absorption) in a three-year trial (Caravia et al., 2016).

When a shade-tolerant crop is cultivated under the photovoltaic panels the negative effects on productivity are very limited, in particular in the case of stilt-mounted agrivoltaic systems (Sekiyama and Nagashima, 2019). Increases in plant height below photovoltaic panels have been reported for celeriac (Weselek et al., 2021b) and potato and winter wheat (Weselek et al., 2021b), as consequence of artificial shading since photovoltaic panels reduced PAR by 30% on two-year average (Weselek et al., 2021b). A general sustained vegetative growth, as indicated by the higher pruning weight in the first season, because of the reduced available light, can be considered an adaptation of the vines to shaded environments (either tolerance or avoidance) in order to increase light

capture interpreted as a shade-adaptive response aimed at enhancing light adsorption (Gommers et al., 2013; Ruberti et al., 2012). In the research by Greer and Weedon (2012b), no difference was observed for the length and the dry weight of vine stems grown in low light intensity with respect to vines in full light. In fact, the water distribution into shoots under shaded condition may extend shoot growth, increase the vine’s water capacitance during periods of transpiration demand, and enhance nutrient acquisition. All these conditions can maintain fruit development without (or very low) detrimental effect on yield (Neri et al., 2003), which can explain the limited difference between AV and FS vines on some yield parameters. However, if the radiation reduction is below 30– 40% no significant effects on plant growth and quality can be observed, otherwise with a deep coverage with the panels ( _>_ 60%) negative effects will be significant, but the recent photovoltaic panels allow enough PAR to reach the plants.

The data on productivity of this vineyard in Northern Italy are promising for application of photovoltaic panels above a wine grape vineyard because of the limited effects on yield but, in conditions with limited water availability, intense solar radiation, and high temperatures the negative effects of the shade on yield can be much reduced as observed in celeriac (Weselek et al., 2021b) and other species and even with positive effects on yield. Cultivation of crops like grapevines or other fruit tree species could be considered profitable in dry and hot weather conditions with more stable yield during the years, as reported for vegetable crops in hot and dry seasons in Central Europe (Weselek et al., 2021a, b) or for apple in France (Juillion et al., 2022). In a dry environment, the yield of tomatoes almost doubled when grown under photovoltaic panels in the field with respect to full sun grown tomatoes (Barron-Gafford et al., 2019).

In a 62% light reduction of a Shiraz vineyard, shaded berries had lower pH and higher TA with respect to control vines (Caravia et al., 2016). High TSS concentration has a strong effect on the fermentation process and wine composition, because of the variations on sensory parameters and microbiological activity, and these effects are accentuated in warm seasons with a negative impact on wine composition and overall quality (Cataldo et al., 2022). The use of shading nets significantly reduced the TSS but increased the TA in Sauvignon blanc grapes (Cataldo et al., 2022). The lower TSS content maybe also a possible consequence of a larger amount of water in the AV berries with respect to the FS ones because of the reduced water loss. In the case of strawberry, both the chlorophyll content of the shaded leaves and the TSS content in the fruits under the panels were higher than that of the unshaded strawberries (Tang et al., 2020), differently from our results.

Papers referring to the shade effects of the photovoltaic panels on the polyphenols are almost nil, although many papers have investigated the effects of different shadings on the polyphenolic content of grapes and gene expression (Bergqvist et al., 2001; Spayd et al., 2002; Ristic et al., 2007; Gao et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2017; Ghiglieno et al., 2020). The cultivation of wild strawberry, blackberry and raspberry in photovoltaic greenhouses with 32 and 100% cover ratio (semi-transparent and non-transparent modules, respectively) increased the antioxidant activity of the fruits, including total anthocyanins, citric and fumaric acid but reduced the sugar content (Blando et al., 2018). A general lower accumulation of anthocyanins, polyphenols, tannins and epicatechin has been reported in shaded Shiraz berries with respect to control vines (Caravia et al., 2016) as observed in our trial. Vines in AV vineyard presented a higher content of non-acylated anthocyanins and lower amount of acylated ones (Table 5). Acylated anthocyanins have higher stability and antioxidant activity compared with non-acylated ones (Hu et al., 2014) and are more stable in aqueous solutions and are of interest to the food and beverage industry (Galaffu et al., 2015), but the bioavailability of anthocyanins as such is extremely low and acylation decreases it even further (Jokioja et al., 2021).

The application of shading treatment can affect temperature, radiation and humidity within grapevines canopies (Haselgrove et al., 2000) and consequently decrease plant transpiration and stomatal

conductance thus affecting the final fruit composition and quality (Downey et al., 2006). In shaded canopies, there is a general decrease in carbon fixation, which resulted in lower levels of some fruit components such as soluble solids, total anthocyanins and polyphenols (Janice et al., 1990) but also in transpiration, stomatal conductance, photosynthesis, stomatal density, hydraulic conductivity, and water use efficiency (Mathur et al., 2018; da Silva et al., 2019), and a similar pattern was observed for the vines under the panels. However, reduced light availability has no effect on vine phenology such as budbreak, full bloom or ripening (Greer and Weedon, 2012b), at least in climates with high temperatures in the final stages of ripening.

During hot, arid, stressful summers, as often occurring in Mediterranean climate conditions, shaded vines can decrease susceptibility to photo-inhibition because of either higher efficiency of the photosystem II or photochemical quenching (Dinis et al., 2018), probably due to an enhanced sucrose concentration in leaf, sucrose transport, and phloem loading aptitude (Conde et al., 2018). Thus, in severe water stress conditions occurring in summer in wine grape vineyards, the shade of the photovoltaic panels could prevent the integrity of the photosynthetic activity of the leaves (Cataldo et al., 2022) thus providing sustainable productions. Moreover, the application of protein hydrolysates (Boselli et al., 2019), use of wastewaters for irrigation (Bedbabis et al., 2014), remote sensors (Torres et al., 2017), or even cover crops (Gattullo et al., 2020) can be other tools to better face climate changes in agriculture coupled with the presence of photovoltaic panels.

A recent techno-economic analysis of application of photovoltaic panels in a vineyard in India showed that the economic revenue increased more than 15 times when compared with traditional grape cultivation considering a similar grape production in the two systems (Malu et al., 2017). Even if considering a reduction in grape production, the great beneficial for energy production in times of high energy demand would be priceless in countries facing high energy needs. Moreover, the yield reduction is very limited under photovoltaic panels and in many areas characterized by high temperatures and water scarcity (i. e., Mediterranean basin) yield can be even higher towards a more sustainable management of the vineyard. For agricultural products such as wine, the mitigation on temperature of grapes can have also positive effects on the quality of the product as for acidity, aromatic compounds, tannins, etc.

A possible application for sustainable orchards could be the use of modern solar tracking photovoltaic systems for energy production without competing with food production in hot, dry and marginal areas thus allowing both food and energy production. Photovoltaic panels may be coupled with fruit tree species (fig, pomegranate, etc.) less susceptible to water scarcity (Ferrara et al., 2014, 2016) in many agricultural areas of the world. Since shading nets are proposed in viticulture as a tool to face the high temperatures (global warming) and limit evapotranspiration (Naulleau et al., 2021), the presence of the photovoltaic panels could act in the same way but providing renewable energy. Moreover, we can also add the elimination of the costs for the disposal of such nets and plastic materials towards a more sustainable environment.

## **5. Conclusion**

Grapevines cultivated below photovoltaic panels in an AV system were affected to a various extent by the effects of the shade depending on the parameter examined. The most positive effects were observed around midday when the highest temperatures were reached during summer. In general, AV vines had a lower metabolic activity in the morning with respect to FS vines but around midday performed much better. Transpiration and photosynthesis were reduced but vines faced less negative ψstem, which is very positive in water limiting conditions. Vine yield reduced more as cluster weight than berry weight, whereas pruning weight was almost the same both for AV and FS vines. TSS together with polyphenols and anthocyanins were lower in AV grapes

but the content of organic acids was higher, and this is important for white grapes grown in hot climates.

As a co-productive system, the advantages of AV are evident: increased income through additional renewable energy production, conservation of land resources through increased land productivity, and potential benefits for crop production in dry, abandoned, and marginal areas. In some areas, the shading of the photovoltaic panels could be a positive application to avoid excessive temperatures and reduce the amount of incident light to the crops thus reducing water loss, another very important and limiting resource in the new climatic scenarios.
